Malicious litellm_init.pth startup hook dropped in site-packages (CVE-2026-42208) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the credential-stealer `litellm_init.pth` startup hook shipped by the compromised litellm 1.82.7/1.82.8 wheels, which Python auto-executes on interpreter startup with no import. Article-specific because the filename and site-packages location are unique to this supply-chain payload. Rationale: The `litellm_init.pth` filename in `site-packages/` is a unique, high-fidelity artifact of the CVE-2026-42208 payload named directly in the advisory and confirmed by Snyk/NetSPI/BerriAI issue #24512 (34,628-byte .pth). No legitimate package ships a file with this exact name. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24512 • https://snyk.io/blog/poisoned-security-scanner-backdooring-litellm/ • https://www.netspi.com/blog/executive-blog/ai-ml-pentesting/litellm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-42208
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A local security-audit or IR script writing a decoy litellm_init.pth as a canary/test file
  • Backup or file-integrity tooling restoring an archived site-packages tree containing the artifact
  • Developer intentionally reproducing the IOC in a sandbox for research
  • A remediation script quarantining the file to a new path (rename event)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pip","uv.exe") or ActionType == "FileCreated"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256 of the dropped file and the InitiatingProcess (expect pip/python during install); identify which project's requirements pulled litellm 1.82.7/1.82.8. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the litellm_init.pth, and force-rotate every credential reachable from that environment (AWS/GCP/Azure keys, SSH keys, kubeconfig, DB creds, CI/CD secrets). 3) Hunt: search all build agents and dev workstations for the same filename, pin litellm>=1.83.7,!=1.82.8, and pivot to the network beacon UC (models.litellm.cloud) to confirm exfil occurred.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "litellm_init.pth"
| where FolderPath has "site-packages"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "litellm_init.pth"
| where TargetFilePath has "site-packages"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious litellm_init.pth Startup Hook Dropped (CVE-2026-42208)
id: 6f3d1c8a-2b4e-4a1f-9c77-1e2f9a0b7d31
description: Detects creation of the litellm_init.pth credential-stealer startup hook from the compromised litellm 1.82.7/1.82.8 wheels
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-98x5-vq43-vc5p
  - https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24512
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-42208
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1546.016
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\litellm_init.pth'
    TargetFilename|contains: 'site-packages'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\litellm_init.pth OR *\site-packages\* AND *litellm_init.pth)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/litellm_init\.pth$/i | regex("site-packages", field=TargetFileName) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="litellm_init.pth" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where like(file_path,"%site-packages%") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="litellm_init.pth" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where like(file_path,"%site-packages%") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
litellm supply-chain exfil beacon to models.litellm.cloud (CVE-2026-42208) AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections/DNS to models.litellm.cloud, the exfiltration endpoint the compromised litellm wheel POSTs AES-256/RSA-encrypted stolen credentials to. Article-specific because this domain is the hard-coded C2/exfil sink for CVE-2026-42208, not a generic egress heuristic. Rationale: models.litellm.cloud is the exact hard-coded exfil endpoint cited in the advisory and independently confirmed by Snyk, NetSPI, Miggo and BerriAI issue #24512 as the AES-256/RSA POST sink; any resolution of it is a confirmed second-source IOC, not a heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24512 • https://snyk.io/blog/poisoned-security-scanner-backdooring-litellm/ • https://www.miggo.io/post/rce-in-litellm-cve-2026-42208-how-two-vulnerabilities-and-36-hours-turn-an-ai-gateway-into-a-backdoor • https://www.netspi.com/blog/executive-blog/ai-ml-pentesting/litellm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel/EDR product performing sinkhole or reputation lookups against the known-bad domain
  • A SOC analyst manually browsing to the domain during triage
  • A DNS security appliance pre-resolving blocklist entries for enrichment
  • Passive DNS/telemetry-replay tooling replaying historic captures
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the request (expect python.exe/pip) and whether the connection succeeded vs was blocked; correlate the host with the litellm_init.pth file UC. 2) Contain: block models.litellm.cloud and *.litellm.cloud at proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat all locally reachable secrets as compromised — rotate immediately. 3) Hunt: sweep DNS/proxy logs org-wide for any prior resolution of the domain to scope every affected build agent and developer host, and audit CI/CD secret stores for anomalous use of the exposed credentials.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "models.litellm.cloud"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "models.litellm.cloud"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["71e35aef03099cd1f2d6446734273025a163597de93912df321ef118bf135238", "a0d229be8efcb2f9135e2ad55ba275b76ddcfeb55fa4370e0a522a5bdee0120b", "6cf223aea68b0e8031ff68251e30b6017a0513fe152e235c26f248ba1e15c92a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Backpropagate training UI publicly exposed via 'backprop ui --share' (CVE-2026-48797) AIDelivery High
Hunts process executions of the Backpropagate CLI launching the Reflex training UI with the --share (public exposure) or --auth flags. Pre-1.2.0 the --auth control is inert, so any --share launch stands up an unauthenticated training control plane; --share --auth is the false-safety case operators believed was protected. Rationale: Uses the exact CLI invocation surface from the advisory (backprop ui + --share/--auth). --share is the article's documented public-exposure flag and pre-1.2.0 makes the UI reachable with no working auth; matching --auth alongside surfaces the false-safety deployments the advisory calls out. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f65r-h4g3-3h9h • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/backpropagate/CVE-2026-48797/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-48797/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ML engineer intentionally running 'backprop ui --share' behind a VPN/reverse proxy that adds its own auth
  • Post-upgrade (>=1.2.0) hosts where --auth now works but the command line still contains the flag
  • CI/CD or lab automation launching the UI with --share for smoke tests
  • Operator using --share only on a firewalled internal network
  • Shell history / documentation examples echoed into a terminal without actually binding a port
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ci-runner", "jenkins", "buildkite-agent")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host's installed backpropagate version (pip show backpropagate / package inventory) — if >=1.2.0 the auth is enforced and risk is low; if 1.1.0-1.1.1 with --share, treat as an exposed unauthenticated training plane. 2) Contain: kill the Reflex process, block inbound to the bound port (default 7860) at the host firewall, and if the UI was internet-reachable revoke/rotate the operator's HuggingFace token (Hub-push abuse vector). 3) Hunt: pull inbound connections to port 7860 from non-loopback sources, review rx.upload writes for attacker-dropped datasets, and check HF push history for unexpected repo targets.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "backprop" and ProcessCommandLine has "ui"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--share" or ProcessCommandLine has "--auth"
| extend PublicShare = ProcessCommandLine has "--share"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, PublicShare, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetProcessCommandLine has "backprop" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "backprop")
| where (TargetProcessCommandLine has "ui" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "ui")
| where (TargetProcessCommandLine has "--share" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "--auth" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "--share" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "--auth")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Host running vulnerable Backpropagate 1.1.0-1.1.1 (CVE-2026-48797) in software inventory AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces endpoints with the Backpropagate package in the affected 1.1.0-1.1.1 range where the Reflex UI auth guard is inert. This is a posture/attack-surface hunt to prioritise upgrades to 1.2.0 before an exposed UI is reached, keyed on the CVE and the concrete package/version range from the advisory. Rationale: Keys on the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-48797) and the advisory's affected version range (pip:backpropagate >=1.1.0,<1.2.0), so it enumerates the concrete attack surface without guessing behaviour. Vuln-inventory telemetry only, no endpoint noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-48797/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/backpropagate/CVE-2026-48797/ • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-48797-cwe-358-improperly-implemented-secu-63bfdfdd
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already scheduled/queued for the 1.2.0 upgrade in the current patch window
  • Isolated air-gapped GPU boxes where the UI is never launched with --share
  • Dev sandboxes intentionally kept on 1.1.x for reproducibility that never bind the UI
  • TVM version parsing quirks reporting 1.1.x npm @mcptoolshop/backpropagate separately from the pip package
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported version is truly 1.1.0 or 1.1.1 (not a mis-parsed 1.2.x) and whether the host has ever launched the Reflex UI. 2) Contain: schedule/push 'pip install --upgrade backpropagate' to >=1.2.0 (or @mcptoolshop/backpropagate@latest); if immediate upgrade is impossible, ensure the UI is only started with no flags (localhost bind) and reachable only via SSH port-forward. 3) Hunt: cross-reference these hosts against process-creation hits for 'backprop ui --share' and inbound connections to port 7860 to find any that were actually exposed.

Inbound access to exposed Backpropagate Reflex UI port 7860 from non-local source (CVE-2026-48797) AIExploitation Medium
Detects inbound network sessions to the Reflex training UI's default port 7860 originating from non-loopback/non-RFC1918 addresses. On an unpatched host launched with --share this is direct unauthenticated access to the training control plane (dataset read, training start, HuggingFace push), i.e. active exploitation rather than mere exposure. Rationale: Port 7860 is the Reflex/Gradio default the advisory itself references (ssh -L 7860:localhost:7860 workaround). Inbound from a public/non-RFC1918 source to that port on an unpatched host is the concrete exploitation shape for the unauthenticated UI, distinct from the process-launch and inventory pivots. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f65r-h4g3-3h9h • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-48797/
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote collaborator reaching a --share UI over a corporate egress IP that presents as public
  • Other apps that also default to port 7860 (Gradio demos, unrelated Reflex apps) on the same host
  • Vulnerability scanners / attack-surface tools probing 7860 across the estate
  • NAT/proxy hairpin making an internal client appear as a public source IP
  • Load-balancer or uptime-monitor health checks hitting the port
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "reflex", "backprop", "node")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the listening process on 7860 is the Backpropagate/Reflex UI (InitiatingProcessFileName python/reflex) and the host version is 1.1.0-1.1.1; identify the remote source IP and whether it is expected. 2) Contain: block inbound 7860 at host/perimeter firewall, terminate the Reflex process, and rotate the operator's HuggingFace token if the session was reachable. 3) Hunt: review rx.upload file writes and dataset-preview reads during the session window, enumerate any HuggingFace Hub push targets, and check for repeated/high-volume uploads indicating disk-fill DoS.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where LocalPort == 7860
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted", "ListeningConnectionCreated")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstPortNumber == 7860
| where NetworkDirection == "Inbound"
| where isnotempty(SrcIpAddr) and not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)) and SrcIpAddr != "127.0.0.1"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, SrcIpAddr, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Incus daemon (incusd) writes file outside image store to cron/OS path (CVE-2026-48769) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-48769: Incus has an arbitrary file write on its clien
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Incus daemon (incusd) writes file outside image store to cron/OS path (CVE-2026-48769) AIInstallation High
Hunts the arbitrary-file-write primitive of CVE-2026-48769: the incusd daemon creating or modifying a file under a root-executable location (cron dirs, sudoers.d, systemd units, ld.so.preload, root SSH, profile.d) as a result of a path-traversal Incus-Image-Hash header. incusd has no legitimate reason to write into these OS directories, so a hit is a near-certain exploitation of the direct-URL image import. Rationale: Uses the exact daemon binary (incusd), the exact image-store root the traversal escapes (/var/lib/incus/images/), and the root-executable sink directories (/etc/cron.d etc.) named in the PoC (../../../../etc/cron.d/incus-direct-image-url-rce). incusd writing outside its own data dir into an OS boot/cron path is effectively impossible in normal operation, giving a very low FP rate. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-f6m5-xw2g-xc4x • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-f6m5-xw2g-xc4x • https://advisory.eventussecurity.com/advisory/incus-vulnerabilities-break-host-instance-boundary/
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A local admin running incusd with a non-default storage path and image store relocated outside /var/lib/incus (custom Incus config)
  • Incus instance provisioning hooks / cloud-init integration that legitimately drop a profile.d or systemd unit during container start
  • Configuration-management tooling (Ansible/Puppet) invoked under the incusd process tree writing OS files during host bootstrap
  • Package upgrades of Incus itself installing systemd units — attributed to dpkg/rpm, not incusd, but may co-occur
  • EDR mis-attributing a child helper process file write to the incusd parent
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/var/lib/incus" or FolderPath startswith "/etc/incus")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the offending file (FolderPath/FileName) and read its contents — CVE-2026-48769 writes a cron line like '* * * * * root /bin/sh -c <cmd>'. Confirm incusd version (< 6.23.0 = vulnerable) and check recent incus image import with source.type=url. 2) Contain: Delete the planted file, kill any cron/systemd job it spawned, isolate the host, and block/rotate any credentials the payload could reach; snapshot for forensics first. 3) Hunt: Enumerate all incusd file writes outside /var/lib/incus in the last 30d, review incusd outbound HTTP to unknown image servers, and check other hosts running vulnerable Incus for the same planted filenames.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "incusd"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/cron.weekly","/etc/cron.monthly","/etc/crontab","/var/spool/cron","/etc/sudoers.d","/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/profile.d","/root/.ssh","/etc/systemd/system")
| where FolderPath !startswith "/var/lib/incus/images"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has "incusd"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate","FileRename")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/crontab","/var/spool/cron","/etc/sudoers.d","/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/profile.d","/root/.ssh","/etc/systemd/system")
| where TargetFilePath !startswith "/var/lib/incus/images"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Incus daemon outbound image fetch to public host followed by write outside data dir (CVE-2026-48769) AIDelivery Medium
Correlates the delivery and exploit halves of CVE-2026-48769: incusd making an outbound connection to a public IP (the attacker-controlled source.type=url image server) and, on the same host within minutes, writing a file anywhere outside /var/lib/incus. Gating the file-write on a preceding external fetch catches traversal to sinks the sensitive-dir list misses while suppressing normal local activity. Rationale: Ties the two article-specific behaviours: incusd reaching an external image server (source.type=url HEAD/GET) and then writing outside its own /var/lib/incus tree within a short window — the observable signature of the traversal write. Excluding incus's own /var/lib, /var/log and /etc paths keeps only escapes. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-f6m5-xw2g-xc4x • https://advisory.eventussecurity.com/advisory/incus-vulnerabilities-break-host-instance-boundary/
ATT&CKT1105 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate incus image import from a public image server (images.linuxcontainers.org) that coincides with unrelated incusd file activity on the host
  • incusd fetching a public URL image while normal container disk/backup writes land in a non-standard storage pool outside /var/lib/incus
  • Custom storage pool mounted outside /var/lib/incus causing benign incusd writes to appear as 'escapes'
  • Proxy/NAT egress making an internal mirror appear as a public RemoteIP
  • Short-window coincidence of an image pull and a scheduled Incus maintenance write
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith "images.linuxcontainers.org" and RemoteUrl !endswith "linuxcontainers.org"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Inspect the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl incusd contacted — is it a known image mirror or an unknown/attacker host? Read the written file for a cron/systemd/sudoers payload and confirm incusd < 6.23.0. 2) Contain: Remove the planted file, terminate spawned jobs, isolate the host, and block the remote image-server IP/domain at egress. 3) Hunt: Search all hosts for incusd connections to that RemoteIP and for any incusd writes outside /var/lib/incus; audit who issued the 'incus image import' with source.type=url and from which client/API token.

FortiBleed password-spray success burst against internet-facing Fortinet/edge auth AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a single source IP producing a high volume of failed authentications against a Fortinet appliance (SSL-VPN / admin login) followed by a successful login in the same window — the exact 'successful logins shortly after large-volume password failure events' pattern Unit 42 flags for the FortiBleed credential-spraying campaign. Rationale: Implements Unit 42's explicit FortiBleed guidance — audit remote-access logs for successful logins shortly after large-volume failure events — scoped to Fortinet auth via the CIM app values / DeviceVendor='Fortinet'. Threshold + same-window success join is what separates spray-then-compromise from routine VPN typos. Cross-checked with SOCRadar/SecurityWeek FortiBleed reporting and Arctic Wolf's CVE-2024-55591 analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1110.004 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote worker repeatedly fat-fingering an SSL-VPN password then succeeding
  • Misconfigured VPN client or saved-credential loop retrying stale creds before a successful re-auth
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner (Qualys/Tenable) credential checks against the appliance
  • Shared NAT egress IP where many staff log in (inflated failure+success counts from one SourceIP)
  • Password-rotation day causing widespread first-attempt failures followed by success
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<populate watchlist: known scanner + corp NAT egress IPs via a Sentinel watchlist join, not inline>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the CompromisedUser + SourceIP; geolocate SourceIP and check whether the success used MFA and from a known ASN/country. Inspect the failed-user set — many distinct users from one IP = spray, not a typo. 2) Contain: if SourceIP is foreign/unrecognized, force-disable the compromised admin/VPN account, kill active SSL-VPN tunnels, block the SourceIP at the edge, and rotate the credential. 3) Hunt: from that SourceIP/account pivot to post-auth config changes (new admin accounts, sslvpn user groups), jsconsole admin logins, and any config download — feed into the FortiBleed jsconsole and rogue-admin UCs.
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 1h;
let Failed = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("failure","failed") or Message has_any ("login failed","Login failed","authentication failed","ssl-login-fail"))
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetUsers = dcount(DestinationHostName) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
let Success = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("success","succeeded") or Message has_any ("login successful","SSL tunnel established"))
| summarize Successes = count(), CompromisedUser = make_set(DestinationHostName, 20) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
Failed
| where Failures >= 30   // 30 = empirical spray burst floor per source per hour
| join kind=inner Success on SourceIP, TimeGenerated
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, Failures, TargetUsers, Successes, CompromisedUser
| order by Failures desc

FortiGate jsconsole / loopback admin login (CVE-2024-55591 auth-bypass exploitation) AIExploitation High
Hunts the high-fidelity exploitation signature of CVE-2024-55591: administrative logins attributed to the 'jsconsole' interface and/or successful super-admin logins sourced from the device loopback/local IP — the artifact the Node.js websocket auth-bypass leaves when an unauthenticated attacker forges super_admin access on FortiOS/FortiProxy. Rationale: Uses the two corroborated CVE-2024-55591 exploitation artifacts — `ui=jsconsole` in the admin-login record (matched in CommonSecurityLog Message) and super-admin logins from the device loopback/local IP (CIM Authentication.src=127.0.0.1) — reported by Arctic Wolf, watchTowr ('I Am The Super_Admin Now') and Trustwave. Both are near-zero in benign FortiGate operation. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://labs.watchtowr.com/get-fortirekt-i-am-the-super_admin-now-fortios-authentication-bypass-cve-2024-55591/ • https://trustwave.com/en-us/resources/blogs/spiderlabs-blog/cve-2024-55591-fortinet-fortios-fortiproxy-zero-day
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001 T1556
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately running CLI commands through the FortiGate GUI 'CLI console' widget (also tagged jsconsole) — distinguish by source being a real admin IP, not loopback
  • Automation/orchestration tooling (Ansible/FortiManager) driving CLI via the local console
  • Internal penetration test replicating CVE-2024-55591
  • Health-check scripts hitting the management interface from a jump host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the jsconsole/loopback login corresponds to a real admin session — legitimate jsconsole use originates from an authenticated GUI session with a genuine admin SourceIP; exploitation shows loopback/local src and no preceding interactive auth. Check FortiOS version against the CVE-2024-55591 fixed builds. 2) Contain: isolate the device's management interface from the internet, disable/rotate all admin accounts, and capture the running + startup config for IR. 3) Hunt: enumerate admin accounts and sslvpn user groups created/modified after the first jsconsole login, look for `--userfrom`-style audit-record tampering, and any config download/exfil to chain with the rogue-admin and FortiBleed config-extraction UCs.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Message has "jsconsole"
| where Message has_any ("login","logged in","logged-in","admin")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, DeviceExternalID, SourceIP, AdminUser = SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, Activity, EventOutcome, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `ctime(firstTime)` | `ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Authentication.dest) as dest from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app IN ("fortios","fortigate","fortiproxy","ftnt-fortigate") (Authentication.src="127.0.0.1" OR Authentication.src="0.0.0.0" OR Authentication.src="::1") by Authentication.user, Authentication.src

FortiGate rogue super_admin / SSL-VPN account creation following CVE-2024-55591 exploit AIInstallation High
Hunts post-exploitation persistence for the FortiBleed/CVE-2024-55591 chain: creation of new FortiGate administrator accounts (often random usernames) or new SSL-VPN local users / user groups via config changes. This is how attackers convert a one-shot auth bypass into durable, high-privilege access for offline-cracked credential re-use. Rationale: Targets the documented CVE-2024-55591 post-exploit actions — new admin accounts with random names, new SSL-VPN local users and groups — via Fortinet config-change logs (cfgpath system.admin / user.group) and the CIM Change datamodel (action=created, object_category=user). Account creation on an edge appliance is rare and tightly change-controlled, so FP is low. Corroborated by Arctic Wolf and Cyble. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://cyble.com/blog/cve-2024-55591-the-fortinet-flaw-putting-critical-systems-at-risk/
ATT&CKT1136 T1098 T1133
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned admin onboarding by the network team during a change window
  • FortiManager/automation pushing a config template that provisions admin or VPN users
  • Legitimate SSL-VPN user-group expansion during an access-request rollout
  • MSP/managed-SOC provisioning a monitoring admin account
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ActorAdmin and SourceIP that created the new object; correlate against an authorized change ticket and verify the actor session was not a jsconsole/loopback exploit login. Flag random-looking usernames. 2) Contain: delete or disable the unauthorized admin/VPN account and group, terminate its sessions, and rotate credentials for every legitimate admin on the device. 3) Hunt: review whether the new account granted VPN access, established tunnels into internal networks, or downloaded the device config; pivot on its SourceIP across other edge devices to scope the FortiBleed campaign footprint.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Message has_any ("system.admin","user.local","user.group")
| where Message has_any ("super_admin","prof_admin","accprofile","sslvpn")
| where Message has_any ("Object attribute configured","Added","cfgattr","New","create")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, ActorAdmin = SourceUserName, NewObject = DestinationHostName, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Change)`
| `ctime(firstTime)`
| sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, values(All_Changes.user) as actor, values(All_Changes.command) as command from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.action=created All_Changes.object_category=user All_Changes.vendor_product IN ("Fortinet FortiGate","FortiGate","FortiOS","Fortinet FortiProxy") by All_Changes.dest, All_Changes.object

FortiBleed MSSQL login-failure burst then success (internet-exposed SQL spraying) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the FortiBleed campaign's parallel targeting of internet-exposed MSSQL: a single client IP generating a burst of SQL Server login failures (error 18456) across one or many logins within a short window — the spray signature Unit 42 observed against MSSQL devices alongside Fortinet and Sophos. Rationale: Covers the article's explicit observation that the FortiBleed actors also targeted MSSQL devices. Pivots on SQL Server error 18456 (login failed) parsed for CLIENT IP and login name in Sentinel's Event table, with a Defender DeviceLogonEvents fallback for Windows-auth brute force against the SQL host and a CIM Authentication path for Splunk. Threshold-based, so framed as a burst detector. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application/service account with a stale connection string hammering the DB after a password change
  • Linked-server or ETL job misconfigured with wrong credentials retrying in a tight loop
  • Monitoring agent (SCOM/SolarWinds) probing SQL with expired creds
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner credential audit against the SQL instance
  • Developer load-test pointing at the wrong SQL host
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("sqlmonitor","svc-etl","svc-backup")   // tune to your known SQL service accounts
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve ClientIP — internal app server vs external/unknown. Inspect the targeted login set: many distinct logins from one IP = spray; a single service account = likely stale credential. Check for any 18454/successful login from the same ClientIP right after the burst. 2) Contain: if external, block the ClientIP at the firewall, confirm the SQL instance is not directly internet-exposed, and disable SQL-auth logins that were sprayed; enforce that MSSQL sits behind the VPN/jump box. 3) Hunt: if a success followed, review that login's subsequent activity (xp_cmdshell, new SQL logins, linked-server abuse) and pivot the ClientIP across Fortinet edge logs to tie it to the broader FortiBleed spraying infrastructure.
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "LogonFailed"
| where LogonType in ("Network","Batch")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetedAccounts = dcount(AccountName), Accounts = make_set(AccountName, 30), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| where Failures >= 30   // 30 failed network logons / 30 min from one source = spray
| order by Failures desc
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 30m;
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Source == "MSSQLSERVER"
| where EventID == 18456   // SQL Server: Login failed
| extend LoginUser = extract(@"Login failed for user '([^']+)'", 1, RenderedDescription)
| extend ClientIP = extract(@"\[CLIENT: ([0-9A-Fa-f\.:]+)\]", 1, RenderedDescription)
| where isnotempty(ClientIP)
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetedLogins = dcount(LoginUser), Logins = make_set(LoginUser, 30) by ClientIP, Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, window)
| where Failures >= 30
| order by Failures desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("mssqlserver","mssql","sqlserver","microsoft sql server") Authentication.action=failure by Authentication.src, Authentication.user, _time span=30m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(count) as failures, dc(user) as targeted_logins, values(user) as logins by src, _time
| where failures >= 30
| sort - failures
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("mssqlserver","mssql","sqlserver","microsoft sql server") Authentication.action=failure by Authentication.src, Authentication.user, _time span=30m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(count) as failures, dc(user) as targeted_logins, values(user) as logins by src, _time
| where failures >= 30
| sort - failures

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

2026-06-26 4 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

Incus has an argument injection in backup compression algorithm leading to AFW and ACE

ATT&CKT1190

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Incus daemon (incusd) spawns backup compressor with argument-injection flags (--pass-through/-o) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-48755: Incus has an argument injection in backup comp

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Incus daemon (incusd) spawns backup compressor with argument-injection flags (--pass-through/-o) AIExploitation High
Hunts CVE-2026-48755: incusd invokes an allow-listed compressor (zstd/gzip/xz/etc.) for a direct backup passing ONLY '-c', but attacker-controlled compression_algorithm smuggles extra tokens. A compressor child of incusd carrying a file-write flag (--pass-through, -o, --output) is the argument-injection primitive — legitimate compression-to-stdout never uses those. Rationale: Keys on the exact article primitive: incusd (root daemon) → allow-listed compressor whose cmdline carries --pass-through/-o/--output. Backup compression writes to stdout, so these output flags are exclusively the injection payload. Cross-checked GHSA-v6mj-8pf4-hhw4 and Snyk Labs Incus write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-v6mj-8pf4-hhw4 • https://labs.snyk.io/resources/incus-vulnerabilities-newline-symlink-arbitrary-writes/ • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-v6mj-8pf4-hhw4
ATT&CKT1190 T1202
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Newer/patched Incus (>=7.2.0) that has removed the vuln — should no longer emit compressor children with these flags; a hit post-patch warrants investigation
  • Custom operator-defined compression_algorithm using legitimate tuning flags like 'zstd -19 -T0' (does NOT contain -o/--pass-through, so filtered)
  • A wrapper compressor script an admin registered that internally forwards -o for its own output handling
  • Backup restore/import which runs the compressor with '-d' to stdout (no -o), correctly excluded by requiring an output flag
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine contains "/var/lib/incus/backups/")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full CompressorCmd — confirm it contains an explicit output path (-o/--output/--pass-through) pointing at a host location outside /var/lib/incus/backups (e.g. /etc/cron.d/). Note the DeviceName and the Incus version via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host; stop incusd; block API port 8443 at the firewall and revoke any client certs/tokens that authenticated the offending /backups request. Delete any attacker-written host file. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC2 (compressor writing to /etc). Review incusd access logs for POST /1.0/instances/*/backups with anomalous compression_algorithm, and check /etc/cron.d, /etc/systemd/system, /root/.ssh for freshly written entries. Upgrade to Incus v7.2.0.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "incusd"
| where FileName in~ ("zstd","gzip","xz","lz4","lzma","bzip2","pigz","pzstd","pxz","tar2sqfs")
// incusd passes only '-c' (+ optional level/thread) for backup compression; -o/--pass-through/--output are file-write injection primitives
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "--pass-through"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains " -o "
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "--output"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          CompressorImage = FolderPath,
          CompressorCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "incusd"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("zstd","gzip","xz","lz4","lzma","bzip2","pigz","pzstd","pxz","tar2sqfs")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine contains "--pass-through"
    or TargetProcessCommandLine contains " -o "
    or TargetProcessCommandLine contains "--output"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Incus Daemon Spawns Compressor With Argument-Injection Flag
id: 4c8f1a52-7d3e-4b19-9a2c-1f0e6b7d5a01
description: Detects CVE-2026-48755 argument injection where incusd invokes an allow-listed backup compressor carrying a file-write flag (--pass-through/-o/--output) that legitimate compression-to-stdout never uses.
references:
  - https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-v6mj-8pf4-hhw4
  - https://labs.snyk.io/resources/incus-vulnerabilities-newline-symlink-arbitrary-writes/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1202
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '/incusd'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/zstd'
      - '/gzip'
      - '/xz'
      - '/lz4'
      - '/lzma'
      - '/bzip2'
      - '/pigz'
      - '/pzstd'
      - '/pxz'
      - '/tar2sqfs'
  selection_flag:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '--pass-through'
      - ' -o '
      - '--output'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_flag
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(zstd OR gzip OR xz OR lz4 OR lzma OR bzip2 OR pigz OR pzstd OR pxz OR tar2sqfs) (@process.command_line:*--pass-through* OR @process.command_line:*--output* OR @process.command_line:*\ -o\ *)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/incusd$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(zstd|gzip|xz|lz4|lzma|bzip2|pigz|pzstd|pxz|tar2sqfs)$/i
| regex("(--pass-through|--output|\\s-o\\s)", field=CommandLine)
| table([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name=incusd (Processes.process_name IN ("zstd","gzip","xz","lz4","lzma","bzip2","pigz","pzstd","pxz","tar2sqfs")) (Processes.process="*--pass-through*" OR Processes.process="* -o *" OR Processes.process="*--output*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name=incusd (Processes.process_name IN ("zstd","gzip","xz","lz4","lzma","bzip2","pigz","pzstd","pxz","tar2sqfs")) (Processes.process="*--pass-through*" OR Processes.process="* -o *" OR Processes.process="*--output*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Backup compressor (child of incusd) writes to a sensitive host persistence path AIInstallation High
Hunts the AFW→RCE stage of CVE-2026-48755: the argument-injected compressor (zstd --pass-through -o ...) lands an attacker file on the host as root. Fires when an allow-listed compressor writes into cron, systemd, sudoers, SSH or profile paths — the PoC drops /etc/cron.d/incus-zstd-rce. A backup compressor writing to /etc is never legitimate. Rationale: Second, independent pivot (file-landing rather than cmdline): a member of the article's exact compressor allow-list writing into /etc/cron.d (the PoC's /etc/cron.d/incus-zstd-rce), systemd, sudoers.d, /root/.ssh or /etc/ld.so.preload. Compressors never legitimately write to these host paths. Corroborated via GHSA-v6mj-8pf4-hhw4 and Snyk Labs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-v6mj-8pf4-hhw4 • https://labs.snyk.io/resources/incus-vulnerabilities-newline-symlink-arbitrary-writes/ • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-v6mj-8pf4-hhw4
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1543.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An admin manually piping a config archive through zstd/gzip into /etc via a shell (rare; check parent is a login shell, not incusd)
  • Configuration-management tooling (Ansible/Salt) that stages a compressed unit file and decompresses it into /etc/systemd/system — verify the invoking user/parent
  • A packaging or backup-restore job that legitimately expands archives into /etc profile scripts
  • Security tooling test/validation writing sample cron files during a controlled exercise
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "incusd"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open the written file (FolderPath/FileName) — a cron entry running '/bin/sh -c', a rogue systemd unit, an added sudoers rule or authorized_keys line confirms RCE/persistence. Confirm the Writer's parent is incusd (InitiatingProcessParentFileName). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, stop incusd, delete the written persistence file, kill any process/cron spawned from it, and rotate root SSH keys and any credentials reachable from the box. Revoke the Incus client cert/token used. 3) HUNT: Correlate with UC1 for the injected compressor cmdline; review /etc/cron.d, /etc/systemd/system, /etc/sudoers.d, /root/.ssh across all Incus hosts; audit incusd for backup requests with crafted compression_algorithm. Patch to Incus v7.2.0.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("zstd","gzip","xz","lz4","lzma","bzip2","pigz","pzstd","pxz","tar2sqfs")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d/","/etc/cron.daily/","/etc/cron.hourly/","/etc/systemd/system/","/etc/sudoers.d/","/root/.ssh/","/etc/profile.d/","/etc/ld.so.preload")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          Writer = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          WriterCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("zstd","gzip","xz","lz4","lzma","bzip2","pigz","pzstd","pxz","tar2sqfs")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d/","/etc/cron.daily/","/etc/cron.hourly/","/etc/systemd/system/","/etc/sudoers.d/","/root/.ssh/","/etc/profile.d/","/etc/ld.so.preload")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Incus S3 multipart uploadId path traversal request (CVE-2026-48753) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound PUT requests to the Incus S3 bucket endpoint whose uploadId query parameter carries directory-traversal sequences (../ or URL-encoded ..%2F), the exploit signature for CVE-2026-48753. This is the on-the-wire primitive that lets an authenticated bucket user write arbitrary host files. Rationale: Anchored on the exact PoC request shape from the advisory: PUT to the bucket with partNumber + uploadId=../../../../etc/cron.d (URL-encoded ..%2F). Traversal in an S3 uploadId has no legitimate use, giving very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-ccjc-4qc3-jxqc • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-ccjc-4qc3-jxqc
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners (Nessus/Burp/Nuclei) firing path-traversal templates against the Incus S3 endpoint
  • Internal red-team / pentest validating CVE-2026-48753 remediation
  • S3 client SDK sending an oddly-encoded but legitimate uploadId that happens to include '..' in a key name (rare)
  • DAST tooling in CI pipelines probing the storage_buckets_address port
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.10.10.10")  // exclude known authorized scanner / pentest source IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target host runs Incus < 7.1.0 with core.storage_buckets_address set; decode the uploadId in RequestURL to see the traversal target (e.g. /etc/cron.d). Identify SourceIP and whether the S3 credentials used are known. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the proxy/WAF, rotate/revoke the storage bucket access keys, and restrict or firewall the S3 bucket port. Upgrade Incus to >=7.1.0. 3) Hunt: pivot to file-write and cron-execution detections on the same host (below) to confirm whether a file actually landed in /etc/cron.d or other sensitive paths.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "PUT"
| where RequestURL has "uploadId" and RequestURL has "partNumber"
| where RequestURL has_any ("..%2F", "..%2f", "../", "%2E%2E%2F", "..%252F")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

incusd process writing to /etc/cron.d or other sensitive host paths (CVE-2026-48753) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Incus daemon (incusd) creating or modifying files under system directories it should never touch — /etc/cron.d, /etc/sudoers.d, /etc/systemd/system, /root/.ssh, ld.so.preload. This is the post-exploitation file-write primitive of CVE-2026-48753 regardless of the specific payload. Rationale: incusd is a storage/container daemon whose legitimate writes stay inside its storage pool directory; any write to /etc/cron.d or /root/.ssh is the exploit outcome. Path list mirrors the advisory's /etc/cron.d target plus adjacent root-RCE sinks. Datadog left empty — the provided linux.auditd schema exposes no file-target path field. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-ccjc-4qc3-jxqc • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-ccjc-4qc3-jxqc
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Incus package upgrade/postinstall touching /etc/systemd/system for its own unit files (verify parent is dpkg/rpm, not incusd itself)
  • Admin manually running incus with elevated config that legitimately regenerates a systemd unit
  • EDR mis-attribution of a helper child process to incusd on busy hosts
  • Backup/restore of a storage volume whose contents coincidentally include cron-like filenames (path would still be inside the pool dir, not /etc)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName != "" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("dpkg","rpm","apt","dnf","yum")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the written file's contents (e.g. /etc/cron.d/*) for a cron line invoking /bin/sh or a reverse shell; confirm incusd version < 7.1.0 and that InitiatingProcess is genuinely incusd, not the package manager. 2) Contain: delete the malicious file, kill any process it spawned, revoke the S3 bucket credentials, and isolate the host. Upgrade Incus to >=7.1.0. 3) Hunt: correlate with the S3 traversal-request detection for the originating SourceIP/credentials, and search for cron-spawned shells or the marker file dropped by the payload across the fleet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "incusd"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/cron.weekly","/etc/cron.monthly","/etc/crontab","/var/spool/cron","/etc/sudoers.d","/etc/systemd/system","/root/.ssh","/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "incusd"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileCreate","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/crontab","/var/spool/cron","/etc/sudoers.d","/etc/systemd/system","/root/.ssh","/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cron-spawned shell that deletes its own /etc/cron.d entry (Incus CVE-2026-48753 payload) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a shell launched by cron whose command line removes a file from /etc/cron.d (self-cleaning run-once cron) or drops the PoC marker file, the execution stage of the CVE-2026-48753 chain where the traversal-written cron job fires as root and cleans up after itself. Rationale: Derived from the advisory PoC cron body: '* * * * * root /bin/sh -c "id > /incus-s3-uploadid-bash-rce; rm -f /etc/cron.d/part-00001"'. A cron job that deletes its own /etc/cron.d file after one run is a strong run-once-exploit tell; the marker string is an exact PoC IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-ccjc-4qc3-jxqc • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-ccjc-4qc3-jxqc
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate provisioning/config-management (Ansible/cloud-init) that deploys a run-once cron.d job which self-deletes
  • Package post-install scripts that clean up transient cron.d drop-ins
  • Admin one-off maintenance cron that removes itself after execution
  • Log-rotation or housekeeping cron that legitimately rm's files under /etc/cron.d during cleanup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","cloud-init","puppet","chef","salt"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ActingProcessCommandLine and any child processes; check whether the executing user is root and whether the cron file originated from an incusd write (correlate with the file-write detection). 2) Contain: if malicious, kill the process tree, remove residual cron.d entries and any dropped marker/payload files, rotate S3 bucket keys, and isolate the host. Patch Incus to >=7.1.0. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the marker file /incus-s3-uploadid-bash-rce and for any other cron.d files written by incusd, and review S3 endpoint access logs for the traversal request that seeded this.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cron","crond")
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "/etc/cron.d/" and ProcessCommandLine has "rm ") or ProcessCommandLine has "incus-s3-uploadid"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("cron","crond")
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "/etc/cron.d/" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "rm ") or ActingProcessCommandLine has "incus-s3-uploadid"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Incus config template read/write primitive abuse (CVE-2026-48752) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the exploitation primitive for the Incus templates/ symlink escape: use of `incus config template create|edit|show` against an instance/image, which — when the image contained a top-level `templates` symlink — reads or writes arbitrary host files as root. Article-specific because it keys on the exact CLI verb chain the PoC uses to trigger host file access. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact PoC verbs (`incus config template create|edit|show`) that are the only interface through which the symlinked host directory is read/written; template use is uncommon enough for a hunt. Cross-checked GHSA-vxp5-584q-c479, DailyCVE and Eventus Security write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-vxp5-584q-c479 • https://dailycve.com/incus-arbitrary-file-read-write-via-unsanitized-symlink-cve-2026-48752-critical-dc-jun2026-681/ • https://advisory.eventussecurity.com/advisory/incus-vulnerabilities-break-host-instance-boundary/
ATT&CKT1611 T1610
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admins authoring cloud-init/config templates on instances via `incus config template edit`
  • CI/provisioning tooling (Packer-style) that ships images carrying templates and edits them post-import
  • Operator running `incus config template show` to audit an existing template
  • Incus documentation/lab walkthroughs exercising the template feature
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and the account; confirm whether the target instance/image was imported from an untrusted tar shortly beforehand and whether the referenced template FILENAME resolves to a host path (e.g. an absolute /etc path) rather than an in-container relative path. 2) Contain: freeze/stop the instance, quarantine the imported image/backup tar, and revoke the user's `incus` group membership pending review. 3) Hunt: check `/etc/cron.d`, `/root/.ssh`, `/etc/sudoers.d`, `/etc/ld.so.preload` for recent writes by incusd, and inventory Incus version — anything < 6.0.6 / 6.21.0 is vulnerable.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "incus"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "config" and ProcessCommandLine has "template"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("create","edit","show")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "incus"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "config" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "template"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("create","edit","show")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

incusd daemon writing to sensitive host paths (Incus templates symlink escape) AIInstallation High
Detects the Incus daemon (incusd, running as root) writing files into privileged host directories that live outside any container storage pool — the concrete host-filesystem escape produced by the templates/ symlink in a malicious image or backup. Article-specific because incusd has no legitimate reason to write /etc/cron.d, /root/.ssh, /etc/shadow, etc. Rationale: incusd is a root daemon whose legitimate writes stay inside the storage pool (e.g. /var/lib/incus); any write it makes to /etc/cron.d, /root/.ssh or /etc/shadow is the direct fingerprint of the symlink escape and the PoC's /etc/cron.d cronjob drop. Datadog left empty — the standard linux.auditd Datadog schema exposes no file-path attribute to pivot on. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-vxp5-584q-c479 • https://advisory.eventussecurity.com/advisory/incus-vulnerabilities-break-host-instance-boundary/ • https://dailycve.com/incus-arbitrary-file-read-write-via-unsanitized-symlink-cve-2026-48752-critical-dc-jun2026-681/
ATT&CKT1611 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Incus host-managed automation that legitimately edits /etc via a custom hook (rare, environment-specific)
  • Storage pool misconfigured to sit under /etc (highly unusual — verify pool path)
  • Backup/restore of a legitimately templated instance whose template path was misconfigured
  • Configuration-management tooling co-located on the host that shares the incusd binary name (verify full path /usr/sbin/incusd)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the written file and its contents — a cron entry running as root, an authorized_keys line, or a /etc/ld.so.preload path is confirmation of exploitation, not a benign write. 2) Contain: remove the malicious file, stop incusd, isolate the host, and rotate any credentials/keys reachable from it; quarantine the source image/backup tar. 3) Hunt: pull the preceding `incus image import` / `incus import` and `incus config template` commands (see companion UC), enumerate all instances created from untrusted images, and confirm Incus is patched to 6.0.6 / 6.21.0+.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "incusd"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/cron.weekly","/etc/crontab","/root/.ssh","/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","/etc/sudoers","/etc/sudoers.d","/etc/ld.so.preload")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "incusd"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/cron.weekly","/etc/crontab","/root/.ssh","/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","/etc/sudoers","/etc/sudoers.d","/etc/ld.so.preload")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Untrusted Incus image/backup import immediately followed by template write AIExploitation High
Correlates an `incus image import` or `incus import` (backup restore) with an `incus config template create|edit` on the same host+user within one hour — the full CVE-2026-48752 exploitation sequence where an attacker imports a tar carrying a templates/ symlink then writes through it to the host. Higher fidelity than either event alone. Rationale: The import (deploy malicious container) followed within minutes by a template write is the complete PoC chain from the advisory; correlating the two on host+user removes the benign-template-edit false positives that UC1 alone carries. Sigma/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty — this is a cross-event temporal correlation not expressible as a single-event rule. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-vxp5-584q-c479 • https://dailycve.com/incus-arbitrary-file-read-write-via-unsanitized-symlink-cve-2026-48752-critical-dc-jun2026-681/
ATT&CKT1610 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated provisioning that imports an image then applies a cloud-init template in the same run
  • Operator restoring a backup and immediately editing its config template legitimately
  • Golden-image build pipeline on a dedicated Incus host that always imports+templates in sequence
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the imported tar's origin and whether it contains a top-level `templates` entry that is a symlink (tar -tv); inspect the template FILENAME argument for an absolute host path. 2) Contain: stop and quarantine the instance and the source tar, revoke the user's `incus` group access, and snapshot the host for forensics. 3) Hunt: run the incusd sensitive-path-write UC to confirm host-side impact, review all images/backups imported by the same user, and verify/patch the Incus version to 6.0.6 / 6.21.0+.
let Window = 1h;
let Imports = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "incus"
    | where (ProcessCommandLine has "image" and ProcessCommandLine has "import") or (ProcessCommandLine has "import" and ProcessCommandLine has ".tar")
    | project ImportTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ImportCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents

| where AccountName !endswith "$"

| where Timestamp between (ImportTime .. ImportTime + Window)
| project ImportTime, TemplateTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ImportCmd, TemplateCmd = ProcessCommandLine
| order by TemplateTime desc
let Window = 1h;
let Imports = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName has "incus"
    | where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "image" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "import") or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "import" and ActingProcessCommandLine has ".tar")
    | project ImportTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ImportCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "incus"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "config" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "template"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("create","edit")

| where TimeGenerated between (ImportTime .. ImportTime + Window)
